name: AI for Photography
objectives: Using your phone camera, take a sharp, well-lit photo by cleaning the lens, holding steady, using good light and tapping to focus, keeping the best of a few shots
Given a photo on your phone, improve it with automatic enhance, cropping and straightening, and undo with Revert if you change your mind

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Taking a clear photo with your phone
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take a sharp, well-lit photo with your phone.
This lesson builds toward: Using your phone camera, you will take a sharp, well-lit photo by cleaning the lens, holding steady, using good light and tapping to focus, keeping the best of a few shots. Given several photos to share, you will create an album or message and share it with a family member, after asking permission for photos of other people.
Good photos start with a few simple habits. Wipe the camera lens gently with a soft cloth; fingerprints make photos blurry. Hold the phone with both hands and keep your elbows close to your body for steady shots.
Light matters most. Face your subject toward a window or daylight, with the light behind you, not behind them. Tap the screen on the person's face or the flower you want to be sharp; the camera focuses there.
Get close, and fill the picture with what matters. Take a few photos instead of one; you can keep the best and delete the rest. Always ask people, especially grandchildren's parents, before you share their pictures.
Step by step:
- Wipe the lens with a soft cloth.
- Hold the phone with both hands.
- Put the light behind you, facing your subject.
- Tap the screen where you want it sharp.
- Take a few shots and keep the best.
Words to know:
- Lens: the small round glass on the back of the phone that the camera sees through.
- Focus: making part of the photo sharp and clear.
Try it now: Wipe your lens, then take three photos of a flower, pet or object near a window. Tap to focus on each one. Look at them and pick your favorite.
You can now take a clear, well-lit photo with your phone.

check.q: Why tap the screen on a face before you take the photo?
options: It focuses the camera on that spot
check.why: Tapping the screen tells the camera where to focus so that spot is sharp.

check.q: You are photographing your friend indoors. Where do you stand?
options: With the window behind your friend
With the window behind you, so light falls on your friend
check.why: Light should face your subject, with the light behind you, not behind them.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Automatic enhance and simple edits
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Improve a photo with one-tap enhance, cropping and straightening.
This lesson builds toward: Given a photo on your phone, you will improve it with automatic enhance, cropping and straightening, and undo with Revert if you change your mind.
Your photo app has an Edit button. Open a photo and tap Edit. Most apps have a one-tap automatic button, often shown as a magic wand, that uses AI to fix brightness, color and contrast in a second.
Next, crop to cut away empty space and straighten a tilted horizon. Look for the crop tool (often a square with arrows), drag the corners in, and rotate a little if needed.
Edits usually do not destroy your original. Most apps let you go back with Revert or Undo. Tap Done or Save when you are happy.
Step by step:
- Open the photo and tap Edit.
- Tap the automatic or magic wand button.
- Use the crop tool to cut empty space.
- Straighten if the picture tilts.
- Tap Done or Save; use Revert if you change your mind.
Words to know:
- Enhance: automatically improving brightness and color in a photo.
- Crop: cutting away the edges of a photo.
Try it now: Open your favorite photo from Lesson 1. Use automatic enhance, crop it a little, and save it. Then compare it to the original.
You can now improve a photo with automatic enhance, cropping and straightening.

check.q: What does cropping a photo do?
options: Cuts away the edges and empty space
check.why: Crop cuts away empty space so the picture is filled with what matters.

check.q: You made edits and now the photo looks worse. What do you do?
options: Tap Revert or Undo to go back
check.why: Edits usually do not destroy the original; Revert or Undo brings it back.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: AI tools that remove distractions
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Remove a small distraction from a photo with an AI eraser tool, and know when edits should be shared honestly.
This lesson builds toward: Given a photo with a small distraction, you will remove it with an AI eraser tool and be honest about how the photo was edited, without changing what really happened in a misleading way.
Many newer phones and photo apps include an AI eraser: you circle or brush over something small you do not want, like a trash can, a stranger in the background or a power line, and the AI fills in the space.
Look in the Edit screen for a tool called something like Magic Eraser, Clean Up or Object Eraser. Names differ by phone, and some phones do not have it. If yours does not, ask an AI assistant: "How do I remove an object from a photo on my phone?" and tell it your phone model.
Small clean-ups are fine for family photos. But do not use AI to change what really happened in a photo in a way that could mislead people, and be honest if someone asks whether a photo was edited.
Step by step:
- Open the photo and tap Edit.
- Look for an eraser or clean-up tool.
- Brush or circle the small distraction.
- Check the result and save, or undo.
- Be honest about edited photos.
Words to know:
- AI eraser: a tool that removes an object from a photo and fills in the background.
- Mislead: to make someone believe something that is not true.
Try it now: Find a photo with a small distraction. Look in Edit for an eraser or clean-up tool and try removing it. If your phone does not have one, ask an AI assistant how to do it on your model.
You can now use an AI eraser tool to clean up a photo, and use it honestly.

check.q: What does an AI eraser do?
options: Removes a small thing you brush over and fills in the space
Makes the photo black and white
check.why: You brush or circle a small distraction and the AI fills in the space.

check.q: Your grandson asks whether you edited the beach photo. You removed a trash can. What do you say?
options: Say no, it was never edited
Be honest that you removed a trash can
check.why: Small clean-ups are fine, but be honest if someone asks whether a photo was edited.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding photos by searching
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find old photos by typing a word in your photo app's search.
This lesson builds toward: Given a photo library with many pictures, you will find photos by searching for a thing, place or date, and mark favorites, finding two older photos without scrolling.
If you have thousands of photos, scrolling is tiring. Photo apps such as Apple Photos and Google Photos use AI to recognize what is in your pictures, so you can search for "dog", "beach", "birthday cake" or "snow".
Open your photo app, tap Search (often a magnifying glass), and type a word. You can also search by place ("Florida") or by month and year ("July 2019"). Many apps can group photos of the same face so you can name people; this is optional, and you can turn it off in settings.
Use favorites to keep your best photos together: tap the heart on a photo, then find all favorites in one album.
Step by step:
- Open your photo app.
- Tap Search or the magnifying glass.
- Type a thing, place or date.
- Tap the heart on photos you love to make them favorites.
Words to know:
- Album: a group of photos kept together, like a page in a photo book.
- Favorites: photos you mark with a heart so you can find them quickly.
Try it now: Search your photo app for two things, such as "flower" and a place you visited. Mark one photo from each search as a favorite.
You can now find old photos by searching and keep your best as favorites.

check.q: How can a photo app find all your pictures of snow?
options: AI recognizes what is in your pictures, so you can search "snow"
It reads the file names you typed
check.why: Photo apps use AI to recognize things in pictures so you can search by a word.

check.q: You want to find photos from your trip in July 2019. What do you type in Search?
check.why: You can search by month and year, by place or by a thing.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making and sharing an album
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Create an album and share it with family.
This lesson builds toward: Given several photos to share, you will create an album or message and share it with a family member, after asking permission for photos of other people.
An album is a collection of photos on one theme, like "Summer at the lake" or "Emma's first year". Making one is a lovely way to share memories.
In most photo apps: select several photos by tapping Select and then each photo, tap the Share button or the plus sign, and choose to add them to a new album or a shared album. Give it a name. A shared album lets family members you invite see the photos, and often add their own.
You can also simply send a few photos in a text message or email. Before sharing photos of grandchildren, ask their parents if it is OK and how widely to share.
Step by step:
- Tap Select and choose several photos.
- Tap Share or the plus sign.
- Choose a new album or shared album and name it.
- Invite family members by name, phone number or email.
- Ask parents before sharing photos of children.
Words to know:
- Shared album: an album that people you invite can see and often add photos to.
- Select: choosing several items at once.
Try it now: Make an album of five favorite photos with a clear name. Share it, or send two of the photos, to one family member.
You can now make a photo album and share it with family.

options: An album that family members you invite can see and often add to
check.why: A shared album lets people you invite see the photos, and often add their own.

check.q: You want to share photos of your granddaughter in a family album. What do you do first?
options: Ask her parents if it is OK and how widely to share
Share them with everyone in your contacts
check.why: Ask parents before sharing photos of children.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Bringing old prints into your phone
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn an old printed photo into a digital copy and improve it.
This lesson builds toward: Given an old printed photo, you will make a digital copy and improve it, labeling any AI-colorized version, with square edges, little glare and the original kept. Given a photo on your phone, you will improve it with automatic enhance, cropping and straightening, and undo with Revert if you change your mind.
Many families have boxes of old prints. You can make digital copies to share and keep safe, using only your phone.
Lay the photo flat near a window, out of direct sun, and take a picture straight from above so the edges look square. Free scanning apps, such as Google's PhotoScan, are made for this and reduce glare. Then use automatic enhance and crop, as in Lesson 2.
Some apps use AI to colorize or repair old photos. These can be fun, but the colors are the AI's guess, not what really happened. Keep the original scan too, and label colorized copies as such when you share them. You can ask an AI assistant to help write a short caption with the names and year.
Step by step:
- Lay the print flat in soft daylight.
- Hold the phone straight above it.
- Take the photo, or use a scanning app to reduce glare.
- Enhance and crop.
- Keep the original; label any AI-colorized copy.
Words to know:
- Scan: making a digital copy of a paper photo or document.
- Glare: a bright shine on a photo from light reflecting off it.
- Colorize: adding color to a black-and-white photo.
Try it now: Final task: take three new photos of something you love, improve the best with enhance plus one other edit, find two older photos by searching, and share all three in a small album or message with family. If you have an old print, add a scanned copy too.
You can now take, improve, find, organize and share photos, including copies of old family prints.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear photos Photos are blurry or dark, or a person was photographed without asking. Three sharp, well-lit photos, with permission from any person in them. The subject fills the frame and the best shot was chosen from several. Photo improved No edits, or edits made the photo worse. The best photo improved with automatic enhance and one other edit, such as a crop. Can show how to revert the edit and explain why they chose it. Old photos found Found photos only by long scrolling, or not at all. Found two older photos using Search with a thing, place or date. Marked favorites so they are easy to find again. Shared with family Photos were not shared, or shared without permission. All three photos shared in a small album or message with a family member. Gave the album a clear name and invited family to add photos. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is glare on a photo of a print?
options: A bright shine from light on the photo
check.why: Glare is a bright shine; scanning apps like PhotoScan help reduce it.

check.q: An app colorized your parents' wedding photo. How do you share it?
options: Say it was always in color
Label it as colorized and keep the original scan
check.why: AI colors are a guess, so label colorized copies and keep the original.
